Human sellers showed the largest block advantage, improving markedly from the Instructed to Natural Preference block (∆M = 0.259, SE = 0.016, p < .001). LLMs showed much weaker block shifts: Llama improved slightly (∆M = 0.039, p = .019), Centaur did not reliably improve (∆M = 0.021, p = .211), and GPT-5 showed a borderline decrease in similarity (∆M = -0.032, p = .050). As a result, the Natural Preference block reversed the human-LLM comparison. In the Instructed block, all three models exceeded human sellers in offer similarity (Llama: ∆M = 0.078; Centaur: ∆M = 0.071; GPT-5 : ∆M = 0.171; all p < .001). In the Natural block, all three models fell below the human baseline (Llama: ∆M = -0.142; Centaur: ∆M = -0.167; GPT-5 : ∆M = -0.120; all p < .001). The LLM-only model did not support a three-way interaction among block, model, and information type (F (6, 41404.4) = 1.94, p = .071). Nevertheless, gaze increased offer similarity relative to Choice alone for every model in both blocks (all p < .001), whereas RT+Choice produced smaller and less consistent gains. We conclude that LLMs can exploit explicit behavioral cues, but humans benefit more from naturalistic preference structure, consistent with stronger use of prior experience and social knowledge.

LLMs recover preferences less accurately than humans

While offering high-utility items demonstrates implicit learning, it remains unclear whether LLMs form accurate, explicit representations of the hidden preferences. We tested explicit state recovery by prompting Llama and GPT-5 to guess the exact numerical attribute weights of the buyer.

Centaur was excluded from this analysis because it reliably returned only a single choice letter and did not produce parseable continuous weight estimates. We quantified accuracy via Pearson correlation (r) with the true weights (Figure 5a).

Interestingly, while human sellers exhibited a robust positive correlation in the Instructed block (r = 0.480), the LLMs' final available estimates struggled to recover weights from choice history alone (Llama: r = -0.004; GPT-5 : r = 0.197). Mixed-model estimated mean differences confirmed that both models remained below human sellers in explicit weight recovery in the Instructed block (Llama: ∆r = -0.378, SE = 0.024, t(3453.5) = -15.46, p < .001; GPT-5 : ∆r = -0.150, SE = 0.027, t(4056.0) = -5.49, p < .001), with similarly large gaps in the Natural block. Thus, the models' high-utility offers do not imply that they recovered the buyer's latent weights in a human-like way. Providing gaze information improved explicit inference considerably. In the Instructed block, Gaze+Choice improved final weight similarity relative to Choice for both Llama (∆r = 0.278, p < .001) and GPT-5 (∆r = 0.226, p < .001), and RT+Gaze+Choice showed similar benefits (Llama: ∆r = 0.240; GPT-5 : ∆r = 0.239; both p < .001). Trial-wise mixed-model trends showed that gaze conditions produced the steepest improvements over repeated attempts (Figure 5b), whereas Choice alone showed no reliable trial-wise increase for either model. This reveals a discrepancy between LLMs' comparatively weak ability to infer hidden preferences explicitly and the superior offers they made (Figure 2), pointing to their computational advantages as well as humans' difficulty translating preference knowledge into optimal choices.

GPT-5 offers align most closely with humans

Finally, while LLMs might achieve high utility, they could do so using decision policies that are very different from human intuition. To test whether the offer profiles of LLMs structurally align with human bargaining behavior, we evaluated exact human-match accuracy (the proportion of trials the LLM selected the identical offer as the human). This analysis distinguishes overall task success from similarity to human behavior.

Raw human-match rates exceeded the attempt-adjusted chance expectation for all models (pooled expectation 9.3% across retained trials; all secondary Poisson-binomial tests p < .001), with GPT-5 achieving the highest raw alignment at 14.0% (Figure 6a). A logistic mixed model confirmed reliable effects of LLM (χ 2 (2) = 84.83, p < .001), Information Type (χ 2 (3) = 161.71, p < .001), and their interaction (χ 2 (6) = 67.47, p < .001). Estimated log-odds differences showed that GPT-5 aligned more closely with human choices than both Llama (∆ = 0.157, SE = 0.025, z = 6.23, p < .001) and Centaur (∆ = 0.271, SE = 0.026, z = 10.54, p < .001), while Llama also exceeded Centaur (∆ = 0.114, p < .001). To contextualize these similarities, we generated a two-dimensional multidimensional scaling (MDS) embedding of pairwise cosine distances between agent offer vectors (Figure 6b). In this projection, the human seller appeared closest to GPT-5 in the Choice condition, and the GPT-5 conditions generally occupied the same upper region of the space as the human point. However, information type also produced substantial within-model separation, indicating that the geometry of offer profiles reflected both model identity and the behavioral cues provided.

The multi-attribute bargaining task suggested that LLMs use RT substantially less effectively than humans, but this result might depend on the task or on how RT was represented. We therefore tested RT-based preference inference in two complementary paradigms. We first used the Konovalov-Krajbich classical bargaining task, an independent bargaining setting in which human sellers received a more explicit temporal signal. We then tested the complementary dictator paradigm, which removes bargaining and asks observers to recover social preferences from RT, choices, or both.

LLMs miss human RT adaptation in classical bargaining

We tested RT sensitivity in the classical bargaining task of Konovalov and Krajbich (23). Offers were made on a 0-100 experimental-currency scale and are reported here in points. For each eligible rejected first offer, a model generated a second offer twice: once without the buyer's RT and once with the same RT stated explicitly. Holding the bargaining event fixed isolates the effect of adding numerical RT to the model prompt. In the human data, the estimated slope relating RT to the second offer changed from -1.060 points when RT was hidden (95% CI [-2.087, -0.044]) to 2.363 points when it was visible (95% CI [0.545, 4.226]). The visible-minus-hidden change was 3.423 points (95% CI [1.340, 5.566], p < .001; Figure 7a).

None of the models showed a comparable increase in RT sensitivity. The visible-minus-hidden changes were -0.270 points for Centaur (95% CI [-0.454, -0.090], p = .003), -0.177 points for Llama (95% CI [-0.474, 0.111], p = .240), and 0.271 points for GPT-5 (95% CI [-0.302, 0.887], p = .366). Direct model-human contrasts confirmed that the RT-sensitivity change was smaller for Centaur (∆ = -3.693, p < .001), Llama (∆ = -3.600, p < .001), and GPT-5 (∆ = -3.152, p = .002). Together, these results reproduce the central RT difference in a distinct bargaining paradigm and response format.

RT increases preference recovery more for humans than for LLMs

We next adapted the preference-estimation paradigm of Bavard et al. (2). Human observers and three LLMs estimated each of 16 dictators' preferred allocation of money between themselves and an anonymous other person on a scale from 0 (giving all money away) to 1 (keeping all money). Estimates were made after seeing allocation pairs with no behavioral outcomes, RTs alone, choices alone, or both RTs and choices. Estimation accuracy generally increased after behavioral observations (Supplementary Figure S2). Because low absolute error can also result from estimates clustered near the center of the scale, preference recovery was defined as the slope relating final estimates to dictators' true preferences.

In a mixed-effects analysis of the None and RT-only conditions, the true-preference × agent × information interaction was reliable (χ 2 (3) = 8.99, p = .029). The model-estimated RT-minus-None increase in preference-recovery slope was 0.308 for humans, compared with -0.267 for Llama, 0.036 for Centaur, and -0.162 for GPT-5 (Figure 7b). The prespecified primary contrast showed that the human increase exceeded the equally weighted mean change across the three models by 0.439 (95% CI [0.138, 0.739], t(344.5) = 2.87, p = .004). Thus, RT increased preference recovery substantially more for humans than for the evaluated models collectively.

Humans recovered preferences from RT alone (r = 0.844, p < .001), whereas the corresponding model correlations were smaller (Llama: r = 0.425, p = .403; Centaur: r = 0.569, p = .086; GPT-5 : r = 0.564, p = .091; all p-values Bonferroni-adjusted; Supplementary Figure S1). Choices alone supported strong descriptive preference recovery for every model (r = 0.764-0.984, all adjusted p ≤ .002), as did RT+Choice (r = 0.916-0.979, all adjusted p < .001). Together, these descriptive correlations show that choices supported strong preference recovery by the models, whereas the mixed model identifies a substantially larger gain from RT for humans.

Discussion

The ability to infer hidden knowledge, beliefs, and preferences from sparse evidence is a strong human social skill, and the development of human-like and supportive AI systems will critically depend on this ability. Here, we tested whether and how current LLMs can infer people's hidden preferences through repeated social interactions. Our central finding is that models can make effective offers without recovering preferences in a human-like way. This dissociation depends strongly on the kind of behavioral evidence available. In the multi-attribute bargaining task, the models improved their offers when they observed previous choices, and gaze information produced particularly strong improvements in preference alignment. Its effect on utility, however, differed across models. By contrast, the models used RTs much less effectively than human sellers did. This qualitative limitation also appeared in two additional paradigms: models recovered preferences much more reliably when choices are available than from RT alone, and do not reproduce the RT-dependent offer adaptation observed in human sellers. Thus, LLMs show a meaningful capacity for interactive preference inference, but this capacity is selective rather than general.

A central goal of our study was to go beyond decision outcomes and investigate whether LLMs take decision processes into account. RT and gaze are informative about hidden preferences in human decision making (24, 27, 28), and humans use these cues when inferring other people's preferences (2, 3, 22). RT posed the clearest limitation for the models. Humans can treat hesitation as a graded signal of conflict or near-acceptance (24), whereas the LLMs showed little evidence of robustly using this implicit process cue. In the Konovalov-Krajbich classical bargaining task, making RT visible did not produce the change in offer sensitivity shown by human sellers. The dictator task reinforced this contrast: RT increased preference recovery substantially more for humans than for the evaluated models. By contrast, first fixations are explicit and easily verbalized: they identify a particular attribute that may matter to the buyer. All models could translate this information into higher-value offers and better explicit weight estimates. However, they tended to adjust more strongly to gaze than human sellers did, and their performance was sensitive to whether the relevant attribute was directly named in the prompt. This suggests that the models' successful use of gaze partly depends on the linguistic framing of the cue. The broader pattern is therefore that LLMs use clear, instructed, textually salient behavioral signals much more effectively than continuous and indirect ones.

An important implication of our work is that high task performance should not be equated with human-like preference inference. All three models, but most notably GPT-5 , produced offers with high utility, and in most cases exceeded the human seller baseline. Yet, explicit weight recovery remained below human performance, and the alignment with human sellers was limited. The markedly better offers in the Natural compared to Instructed Preference block further suggests that prior expectations about plausible human preferences helped humans more than machines, consistent with evidence that prior preferences can improve social and non-social learning (29).

Together, these results indicate that making accurate inferences about hidden preferences and turning these inferences into appropriate actions are separable skills, with humans and AI systems exhibiting complementary advantages. Critically, this insight can help to promote future human-AI synergies. Extensive prior knowledge and sophisticated social inference capabilities on the human side could be combined with the superior quantitative skills of AI systems to obtain the best results overall (30, 31). S1 and S2.

In comparing the open-source models, Centaur showed no reliable average utility advantage over its Llama base model and aligned less closely with exact human choices. It also showed no consistent advantage on the process-sensitive measures of adaptive preference inference central to the present task and was outperformed by GPT-5 . The two additional studies extend this test beyond the multi-attribute bargaining task: Centaur did not show a consistent advantage over Llama in using RT to recover preferences or adjust offers. This does not imply that cognition-specific fine-tuning is unhelpful in general, but it does suggest that training on large collections of isolated choices is not sufficient to produce flexible, human-like social inference. In the present tasks, GPT-5 's broader general-purpose language and reasoning capabilities (12) appeared more useful than choice-based behavioral tuning alone, although GPT-5 also failed to match human RT use. This is especially relevant for models intended to capture general principles of human cognition, including Centaur, because those principles should hold not only in static choice settings but also when a model must update beliefs about another person over time.

An important direction for future work is to determine when cognition-specific fine-tuning supports generalization beyond the psychological tasks represented during training. In the present domain of sequential social inference, training on isolated choice tasks did not produce a robust advantage when the model had to infer and update another person's preferences over repeated interactions. One possibility is that such social-inference tasks were insufficiently represented in the training data. This could be tested by fine-tuning models on related game-theoretic paradigms, including choices and process measures such as RT, eye movements, or mouse trajectories (24, 27, 28, 32), and then evaluating generalization to unseen interactive tasks. If this training failed to outperform larger general-purpose models, it would challenge the value of task-specific behavioral fine-tuning for flexible social inference. If it succeeded, however, it would expose a different limitation: increasingly broad domains and behavioral signals may need to be added before a model can approximate the breadth of human cognition. Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The descriptions and data for the dictator and classical-bargaining studies were public before model inference, so training exposure cannot be excluded. Nevertheless, the evaluated models did not reproduce the human RT-dependent learning effects in either paradigm. As in any text-based LLM study, behavioral evidence must be encoded linguistically before it can be provided to the model. Consequently, the LLMs received an explicit chronological history, symbolic labels of the first-fixated attribute, and, in some conditions, exact numeric RTs, whereas human sellers in the multi-attribute bargaining task relied on a live interface, memory, a dynamic gaze overlay, and the implicit passage of time. These differences qualify direct human-LLM comparisons, but the controlled textual representation also provides a clear test of whether models can integrate distinct process cues across repeated interactions. The Konovalov-Krajbich classical bargaining task narrows this concern: human sellers saw an on-screen timer and, in the RT-visible condition, were notified explicitly when the buyer decided. Nevertheless, the recurring limitation in LLM use of RT across these paradigms strengthens the evidence that it is not specific to the multi-attribute bargaining task. Our findings therefore establish that LLMs can exploit structured descriptions of decision processes and provide a foundation for future work using richer multimodal inputs, including raw gaze and timing signals. While the multi-attribute bargaining task is inevitably a simplified representation of everyday social exchange and omits rich multimodal signals such as facial expressions, verbal cues, and conversational repair, it isolates the core cognitive challenge of adaptive mentalizing: updating beliefs about another's hidden preferences through iterative interaction. Ultimately, integrating sequential behavioral measures into a testing repertoire is crucial.

More broadly, the multi-attribute bargaining task offers a useful complement to standard ToM benchmarks. Vignette-based tasks test whether a model can attribute a belief or intention in a constrained scenario (14, 15, 18), whereas social interaction requires an agent to maintain and revise a representation of another person's preferences from noisy evidence across time. This distinction matters for both cognitive science and human-centered AI. Models that assist, negotiate or adapt to users should not only make good isolated guesses, but should also learn from behavioral feedback in a stable and appropriately calibrated manner. Across three paradigms, the present findings show 2. RT+Choice (Numeric): choice outcomes plus exact RT in seconds (e.g., "Buyer rejected in 2.31 seconds"), accompanied by a reference statement that the buyer makes decisions in 3 s on average.

3. RT+Choice (Descriptive):

choice outcomes plus a qualitative RT label. Rejection latencies below the sample median of 3 s were labeled "Buyer rejected the offer quickly"; latencies at or above this threshold were labeled "Buyer took a long time to reject the offer." The prompt additionally explained the mapping: fast rejections indicate poor preference alignment, whereas slow rejections indicate the offer was close to acceptable. 4. Gaze+Choice: choice outcomes plus the identity of the attribute the buyer fixated first (e.g., "Buyer looked at Speed first and rejected"). The prompt stated that the first-fixated attribute might be the most important to the buyer, instructing the model to offer items with high values on that attribute. 5. Gaze Indirect: choice outcomes plus the identities of the two attributes the buyer did not fixate first (e.g., "Buyer didn't look at Comfort and Safety first and rejected"). This condition conveys logically equivalent information to Gaze+Choice, for which the first-fixated attribute can be deduced by exclusion, but frames the signal in a negated, non-diagnostic manner that avoids directly naming the salient attribute. The accompanying instruction was identical to the Gaze+Choice condition. 6. RT+Gaze+Choice: combined descriptive RT and first-fixation attribute with choice outcomes. Each offer line included both the first-fixated attribute and a qualitative RT label (e.g., "Buyer looked at Speed first and rejected the offer quickly"), together with instructions explaining both signal types.

Each prompt opened with the product category, the three attribute names, and a description of the seller's goal (to infer the buyer's hidden preference weights and propose an acceptable offer). Previous offers and the buyer's reactions were enumerated chronologically, followed by the full list of remaining available options (labeled A-L) and an instruction to select the next offer.

For Llama and GPT-5 , the prompt additionally requested an explicit weight guess in the format Pick: A, Weights: (0.3,0.4,0.3). Prompts were independently adapted for each model family: Centaur was prompted to express its choice as a capitalized letter ("press ⟨X⟩") consistent with its fine-tuning format. In these runs it did not produce parseable continuous weight estimates, so it was excluded from the weight-inference analysis.

The exact prompts used for these conditions are provided in the separate Supplementary Prompt File.

Large language models

Centaur

We used Llama-3.1-Centaur-70B-adapter (8), a low-rank adapter fine-tuned on choice data from an extensive battery of human behavioral experiments. Inference was run locally on a high-performance computing cluster using the Unsloth library (34).

Llama

We used Llama 3.1 70B Instruct (11) as the matched base model, run under identical inference conditions to Centaur.

GPT-5

We used GPT-5 via the OpenAI API (12). Requests were submitted independently for each prompt.

No personal information was revealed to the LLMs.

For GPT-5 runs, temperature could not be varied as a sampling parameter, and we used medium reasoning effort throughout.

All evaluated model checkpoints had been trained before the multi-attribute bargaining task was publicly described, and its trial-level data were not publicly available (8, 11, 12).

The comparable human-model analysis used the 646 eligible rejection events from the second half of the Live experiment (45 human sellers; 320 events in the human RT-hidden condition and 326 in the RT-visible condition). Buyers had 11 seconds to accept or reject each first offer, with an on-screen timer shown during the decision window. The buyer's choice was revealed only when the window ended. In the RT-visible condition, however, the seller was notified as soon as the buyer clicked, allowing decision time to be observed dynamically; in the RT-hidden condition, no such notification appeared. Thus, the human RT signal was more explicit than an unaided sense of elapsed time. For each of these events, both model outputs were retained, yielding 1,292 outcomes per model.

Statistical analysis

Group-level comparisons of utility, offer adaptation, and weight-inference quality were conducted using mixed-effects models implemented in the lme4, lmerTest, and emmeans packages in R (35) (36) (37). Repeated LLM outputs were first averaged within participant × interaction × trial × LLM × condition before inferential modeling. When a human analog was available, human sellers contributed one row per participant × interaction × trial, and estimated mean differences first compared each LLM with the paired human seller data. LLM-only analyses then tested Information Type, prompt format, Preference Block, or trial trends using estimated marginal means or estimated trends with Holm correction within each comparison family. Linear mixed-effects models used random intercepts for participant and repeated-trial units, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom for Type III F -tests and estimated mean differences. For Figure 2a, the same trial structure was used to add two heuristic reference agents: a random-offer agent, defined as the expected utility across all available offers, and an unweighted-sum agent, defined as the offer with the highest total attribute value. For the MDS embedding in Figure 6b, a reproducible random-choice agent selected one of the 12 available offers per trial using a fixed random seed and entered the same pairwise cosine-distance calculation as the other agents. For exact human-match accuracy, binary outcomes were aggregated to hit/miss counts per participant × interaction × trial × LLM × Information Type and analyzed with logistic mixed-effects models. Secondary one-sided Poisson-binomial tests, evaluated with a lattice saddlepoint approximation, assessed whether raw exact-match accuracy exceeded the attempt-specific chance levels (1/12, 1/11, 1/10, and 1/9), calculated from the number of remaining offers in each retained trial. Reported descriptive Pearson r values are used to match figure summaries; inferential claims are based on the corresponding mixed-model estimated differences or trends. Figures display means ± SE; y-axes for utility plots are truncated at 75 to better visualize inter-condition differences while preserving the full distributional structure. For the MDS analysis (Figure 6b), pairwise cosine distances between mean offer vectors were computed over overlapping trials (the Instructed Preference block) and submitted to classical metric multidimensional scaling (cmdscale, k = 2). All statistical analyses and figure generation were performed in R 4.5.2; LLM inference code is written in Python 3.10 using the Transformers and Unsloth libraries.

For the Konovalov-Krajbich classical bargaining task, we estimated second offer as a function of standardized RT, RT visibility, their interaction, standardized first offer, and standardized period.

RT, first offer, and period were standardized using population standard deviations across the 646 eligible events. The estimand was the visible-minus-hidden change in the second-offer slope per one-SD longer RT. Confidence intervals and p-values used 5,000 stratified subject-cluster bootstrap draws. These intervals quantify sampling uncertainty across human subjects, not stochastic variation across model generations.

For the dictator task, descriptive learning curves show mean estimation accuracy across the 16 dictators at checkpoints 0, 4, 8, and 12. Final-estimate inference used all 184 human estimates per condition and the single deterministic estimate for each of 16 dictators per model and condition in the None and RT-only conditions. We fit the maximum-likelihood mixed model estimate ∼ centered true preference × agent × information condition. Correlated condition-specific effects accounted for repeated estimates from each of the 46 human observers, and a random dictator intercept and condition slope accounted for repeated dictators. Model outputs were not replicated. An omnibus likelihood-ratio test compared this model with one omitting the three-way interaction. The prespecified primary contrast compared the human RT-minus-None change in the preference-recovery slope with the equally weighted mean change across Llama, Centaur, and GPT-5. Pearson correlations between final estimates and true preferences within all four conditions are descriptive summaries only; their p-values were Bonferroni-adjusted across the four conditions within each agent.

Data pre-processing and derived variables

Raw LLM outputs were parsed to extract the selected option label (A-L) and, where requested, a three-element preference weight guess. The selected option label was mapped to a row index in the 12-option attribute matrix, yielding a three-dimensional offer vector.

The following derived variables were used in all analyses: • Raw LLM offer utility (u LLM ): the attribute-weighted sum of the selected offer under the buyer's true preference weights.

• Raw human seller utility (u Human ): the same computation applied to the offer selected by the human seller on the matching trial.

• Maximum raw utility (u Max ): the highest utility achievable among the twelve options, given the buyer's weights.

• Utility: u = 100 • u raw /u Max , capped at 100. Unless otherwise specified, utility refers to this normalized definition.

• Offer-preference similarity (Pearson r): the Pearson correlation between an offer attribute vector and the buyer's true preference vector, used to quantify how closely an offer matches the latent preference structure.

• Offer-to-offer similarity (cosine): the cosine similarity between consecutive offer attribute vectors, used to quantify whether consecutive offers target similar preference profiles.

• First-fixation update: the change in the first-fixated attribute's score between the current and subsequent offer, computed for rejected trials in gaze conditions to assess gaze-dependent learning.

• Weight-inference quality (Pearson r): the Pearson correlation between the model's threeelement inferred weight vector and the buyer's true weights, available only for Llama and GPT-5 outputs that contained explicit weight guesses. Cross-agent and preference-block comparisons used the final available estimate in each interaction for both human and LLM sellers; trial-wise analyses retained all estimates from trials 1-4.

• Human-match accuracy: binary indicator of whether the LLM and human seller selected the identical option.

Process-rich interactive paradigms therefore provide a more demanding test of artificial social cognition and a more informative target for models that aim to approximate human cognitive behavior (7, 33).

Multi-attribute bargaining task

The human study used a multi-attribute bargaining task (22) spanning 20 product categories (e.g., cars, laptops, bicycles), each defined by three attributes (e.g., speed, comfort, safety). For each category, the seller viewed a fixed set of twelve product options that varied only in their attribute values (scores on a 0-100 scale). The buyer's utility for any offer was the attribute-weighted sum of its three attribute scores, with attribute weights provided either by the experimenter (Instructed Preference block) or self-generated by the buyer beforehand (Natural Preference block). Weights within each preference vector were constrained to sum to 1, so that all utilities were on a 0-100 scale.

In each product category, the seller selected one of the twelve options to propose; the buyer was then presented with the offer and could either accept or reject it via key press. Rejection prompted a new offer from the seller, with a maximum of four offer attempts per category. If the buyer accepted, they received points equal to the offer utility; if all four offers were rejected, the buyer received a fixed payment of 50 points (so that buyers were incentivized to purchase only attractive options). Sellers received zero points in case of all four offers being rejected and, for successful sales, a performance bonus equal to 0.8 × b + 20, where b is the buyer's utility. This incentive structure encouraged sellers to maximize buyer utility.

Crucially, the sales outcome (accept/reject) was communicated in real time, so the elapsed time between offer presentation and the buyer's key press was implicitly available as a response time. In the Gaze condition, a live gaze overlay on the seller's screen revealed which product attribute the buyer was currently fixating; in the NoGaze condition, sellers received only the binary outcome and its timing.

Gaze coordinates were sampled using an EyeLink 1000 eye tracker and mapped to one of the three attribute regions based on proximity to predefined screen-center coordinates (radius threshold 0.2 in normalized screen units). The attribute whose region was first entered was designated the first-fixated attribute. The buyer was aware that their eye movements were tracked but unaware that this information was shown to the seller (to avoid strategic eye movements), following prior interactive gaze work that emphasizes the strategic consequences of making gaze visible (21).

Participants

A total of 158 participants (79 buyer-seller pairs; mean age = 24.9 years, SD = 6.9; 113 female) were recruited from the University of Hamburg participant pool. All participants were naive to the purpose of the study and gave written informed consent prior to participation. Ethical approval was obtained from the Local Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Psychology and Human Movement Sciences at the University of Hamburg (approval number 2024_010). Each participant received a fixed show-up fee and a performance-based bonus determined by their role and task outcomes.

Participants were randomly assigned to the buyer or seller role and to either the Gaze or NoGaze condition (2 [Condition: Gaze vs. NoGaze; between-subjects] × 2 [Preference type: Instructed vs.

LLM prompt construction

We tested six prompt types reflecting increasing amounts of behavioral process-trace information: 1.

Choice: offer history with binary accept/reject outcomes only (baseline).

Konovalov-Krajbich classical bargaining task

We used the data from the live bargaining experiment of Konovalov and Krajbich (23). The model replaced the seller only at the second-offer stage of rejected first-offer trials. Each prompt stated the first offer, its rejection, the seller's payoff rule, and the requirement to choose a second and final offer from 0 to 100 points on the original experimental-currency scale. Every event was presented in two prompt versions: one omitted RT and the other stated the buyer's observed first-response time numerically in seconds. The prompts were otherwise identical. We generated 2,514 prompts per model from 1,257 eligible events and tested Llama 3.1 70B, Centaur 70B, and GPT-5. The two local models were run at temperature 0; GPT-5 used medium reasoning through OpenRouter and an 8,192-token completion limit. Only exact responses of the form SecondOffer: N.NNN were parsed.

Ethics

All procedures were approved by the ethics committee of the University of Hamburg (approval number 2024_010). All participants gave written informed consent.

Figure 3 :

Figure 3: LLMs use symbolic gaze cues more reliably than response-time cues. a, Binned regression of buyer response time against offer-to-offer cosine similarity for rejected trials (RT+Choice, Numeric encoding), separated by model. Points show bin means (± SE), and lines show linear fits with descriptive Pearson r and p-values. Human sellers showed a clear positive association, GPT-5 showed a weaker positive association, and Llama and Centaur showed no reliable association. b, Mean change in the first-fixated attribute's score across consecutive rejected offers (Gaze+Choice condition), for each LLM, human sellers with gaze, and human sellers without gaze. All three LLMs increased the first-fixated attribute more strongly than human sellers in the gaze condition. c, Mean offer-similarity difference (± SE) between numeric and descriptive RT encoding (Numeric -Descriptive), by model. Exact numeric RTs did not reliably improve alignment for any model. d, Mean offer-similarity difference (± SE) between direct and indirect gaze phrasing (Direct -Indirect), by model. Directly naming the first-fixated attribute improved alignment for Llama and Centaur, but not for GPT-5.

Figure 4 :

Figure4: Humans benefit more than LLMs from natural preference structure. Mean offer-preference similarity (± SE) for each information type, split by preference block, separated by model. Dashed reference lines show human seller similarity for each block, color-matched to preference condition. Human sellers aligned much more closely with buyers in the Natural than in the Instructed Preference block, whereas block differences were small or absent for the LLMs. Consequently, all three LLMs fell below the human baseline in the Natural Preference block. Gaze increased LLM offer similarity relative to Choice alone for every model in both blocks.

Figure 5 :

Figure 5: LLMs recover hidden preference weights less accurately than humans but improve with gaze. a, Mean Pearson r between the final available inferred weights and true buyer preference weights (± SE), by information type, model, and preference block. Horizontal lines show the human seller weight-inference baseline for each block. Both Llama and GPT-5 remained below human sellers, while gaze information substantially improved their explicit weight estimates. Centaur was excluded because it did not produce sufficient parseable weight outputs. b, Mean weight-inference Pearson r (± SE) across trials 1-4, separated by model and information type. Accuracy increased most strongly across trials in the gaze conditions, whereas Choice alone produced no reliable improvement.

Figure 6 :

Figure 6: GPT-5 offers align most closely with human choices. a, Human-match accuracy (LLM-chosen offer = human seller offer) by information type and model. Black dashed line: chance level. All models exceeded chance, with the highest overall match rate for GPT-5, followed by Llama and Centaur. b, Two-dimensional MDS embedding of pairwise cosine distances between agent offer-vector profiles in the Instructed Preference block. Each point represents one agent (LLM × information type); the triangle marks the human seller and the diamond marks a reproducible random-offer agent. The human profile was nearest to GPT-5 with Choice in this projection, while separation among conditions reflected both model identity and information type.

Figure 7 :

Figure 7: Limited RT use by LLMs generalizes across tasks. a, Results of the classical bargaining task. Making RT visible changed human sellers' subsequent offers, whereas Llama, Centaur, and GPT-5 did not show a comparable change. b, Results of the dictator game. RT improved human observers' recovery of dictators' preferences, but did not produce a comparable improvement in the three models. Points show estimated changes and error bars show 95% confidence intervals. Full condition-level results are shown in Supplementary FiguresS1 and S2.

Bavard et al. (2). In Bavard et al.'s original dictator task, 46 observers estimated the preferred self-allocation of 16 dictators. For each dictator, observers saw 12 binary allocation choices under one of four information conditions: allocation pairs without behavioral outcomes (None), decision times without choices (RT), choices without decision times (Choice), or both signals (RT+Choice). Observers reported an estimate on a 0-1 scale after 0, 4, 8, and 12 observations. The LLM adaptation used the same 16 dictators, 12 observations, and four information conditions. Separate prompts requested the dictator's preferred self-allocation after each checkpoint from 0 through 12; checkpoint 0 contained no behavioral observations. Each model therefore completed 832 prompts (16 dictators × 4 conditions × 13 checkpoints). Responses had to contain one numeric estimate from 0 to 1. We tested Llama 3.1 70B, Centaur 70B, and GPT-5. Llama and Centaur were run locally with temperature 0 and seed 20260812; GPT-5 was run through OpenRouter with medium reasoning, excluded reasoning output, and an 8,192-token completion limit. The analyzed table retained complete and prompt-compatible runs only. Estimation accuracy was 1 -|p -p|, where p is the dictator's preferred self-allocation.
